Fix $m\ge1$. A **closed cube** is a rectangle $\prod_{j<m}[a_j,a_j+\ell]$ with $\ell\ge0$; its volume is $\ell^m$. A set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **null** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is covered by a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at most $\varepsilon$. It has **content zero** when such a cover can be finite.

The series and finite sums are [[def-series]] and [[def-finite-sum]], and their nonnegative bounds use [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Both properties pass to subsets. Padding a finite cover with degenerate zero-volume cubes proves that content zero implies null. This terminology defines only cover-nullity; it does not define a measure on arbitrary sets.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

derivations.claim: Choose $x\in O$ and $r>0$ with the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)\subseteq O$. Put $s=r/(2\sqrt m)>0$ and let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^m[x_j-s/2,x_j+s/2]$. For every $y\in Q$, $\|y-x\|_2\le\sqrt m\,s/2=r/4<r$, so $Q\subseteq O$ and $\operatorname{vol}(Q)=s^m>0$.

Suppose $O$ were null. By [F1], with $\varepsilon=s^m/4$ there is a sequence of closed cubes $C_i$ covering $Q$ whose side lengths $\ell_i\ge0$ have $\sum_i\ell_i^m\le s^m/4$. For each $i\ge0$, set $\delta_i=\min\{1,\,s^m2^{-i-5}/(3^m(1+\ell_i)^{m-1})\}$ and enlarge $C_i$ concentrically to an open cube $C_i'$ of side $\ell_i+2\delta_i$. The binomial formula and $\delta_i\le1$ give $(\ell_i+2\delta_i)^m-\ell_i^m\le3^m\delta_i(1+\ell_i)^{m-1}\le s^m2^{-i-5}$. Hence the total enlarged volume is at most $s^m/4+s^m/16=5s^m/16<s^m/2$.
The open cubes $C_i'$ cover the closed box $Q$, so [F2] gives a finite subcover $C_{i_1}',\ldots,C_{i_t}'$. Their total volume is less than $s^m/2$ by step 2.1.

Cut $Q$ and the finitely many covering cubes at all their coordinate endpoints. The positive-side grid cells inside $Q$ partition it; the interior of each cell lies in one covering cube because no covering-cube boundary crosses the cell. Assign each cell to the least index of a covering cube containing its interior. By finite cut-additivity from [F3], the assigned cells for each cube have total volume at most that cube's volume, while all cells sum to $\operatorname{vol}(Q)=s^m$. Thus $s^m\le\sum_{j=1}^t\operatorname{vol}(C_{i_j}')<s^m/2$, a contradiction. Therefore $O$ is not null.

For an integer $D\ge1$ and unit vectors $u,v\in\mathbb C^D$, write $[u]$ and $[v]$ for their pure-state rays and define the projective chord distance by

$$d_{\mathrm{ch}}([u],[v])=\inf_{|\lambda|=1}\|u-\lambda v\|_2.$$

Here $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the norm induced by the root inner product, which is linear in its first argument. The infimum is over unit complex scalars, so it removes only the common phase of a state vector. The companion lemma [[lem-qc-projective-chord-distance-formula]] evaluates this infimum, proves it is attained, gives the closed formula, and proves independence from the chosen unit representatives.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space. Two nonzero vectors $x,y\in H$ represent the same **ray** when $y=\alpha x$ for some nonzero $\alpha\in\mathbb C$. A **pure state** is such a ray. If $u$ is a unit representative, its associated operator is $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$, with the bra, ket and outer-product convention of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]]. The theorem [[thm-qc-ray-projector-well-defined-and-bijective]] proves that this operator is a rank-one orthogonal projection independent of the chosen unit representative, so it is the operator representative of the pure state.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: Put $c=\langle v,u\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$. For every $|\lambda|=1$, expand by [F2]: $\|u-\lambda v\|_2^2=2-\overline\lambda\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}-\lambda\langle v,u\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}=2-2\operatorname{Re}(\lambda c)$.

If $c=0$, the real part is zero for every unit $\lambda$; if $c\ne0$, choose $\lambda=\overline c/|c|$, giving $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda c)=|c|$. Since $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda c)\le|c|$ for every unit $\lambda$, this phase attains the infimum in [F1]; the value is $\sqrt{2-2|c|}$, a real nonnegative number by [F4].

Replacing $u$ and $v$ by unit scalar multiples changes $\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$ by a unit scalar, so its modulus and the displayed value do not change. Since the infimum is attained, it is zero exactly when a minimizing phase satisfies $u=\lambda v$, which is exactly equality of the represented rays by [F3].

For unit vectors $u,v\in\mathbb C^D$,

$$d_{\mathrm{ch}}([u],[v])=\sqrt{2-2|\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}|}.$$

In particular, this value is independent of the chosen unit representatives, and it is zero exactly when the two vectors represent the same ray.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Put $m=D/2$, $x=2\delta\in(0,1/2)$ and $R=\lceil xm\rceil-1$. Greedily scan the finite set $\{0,1\}^m$ in lexicographic order: select the least remaining word and delete all words at Hamming distance at most $R$, repeating until none remain. Distinct selected words have distance $h\ge R+1\ge xm=\delta D$, and each selection deletes at most $B=\sum_{j=0}^{R}\binom mj$ words, so the selected code has at least $2^m/B$ words.

For $j\le R<xm$, the ratio $x/(1-x)<1$ gives $x^j(1-x)^{m-j}\ge x^{xm}(1-x)^{(1-x)m}$. The binomial identity $1=\sum_{j=0}^m\binom mjx^j(1-x)^{m-j}$ therefore yields $B\le[x^{-x}(1-x)^{-(1-x)}]^m=2^{mH_2(x)}$. By [F2], $\ln2=\int_1^2du/u>0$. On $0<t<1$, differentiation gives $H_2'(t)=\ln((1-t)/t)/\ln2$. For $0<t<1/2$, the ratio exceeds $1$, so [F2] gives $\ln((1-t)/t)=\int_1^{(1-t)/t}du/u>0$. Since $H_2$ is continuous on $[x,1/2]$ and differentiable inside, [F3] implies $H_2(1/2)-H_2(x)=H_2'(\xi)(1/2-x)>0$ for some $\xi\in(x,1/2)$. As $H_2(1/2)=1$, we have $H_2(x)<1$. Thus the code size is at least $2^{m(1-H_2(x))}=\exp(c_\delta D)$.

Map each selected bit word $b$ to the sign word $s_i=(-1)^{b_i}$; this is a bijection preserving Hamming distance. Form $u_s=D^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1,s_1,\ldots,s_m)$. It is unit because it has $D$ entries of modulus $D^{-1/2}$. If two selected words differ in $h$ places, then $\langle u_s,u_t\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}=1-2h/D$. Since $h\le m=D/2$ and $h\ge\delta D$, this lies in $[0,1-2\delta]$, so [F1] gives $d_{\mathrm{ch}}([u_s],[u_t])=2\sqrt{h/D}\ge2\sqrt\delta$. The first half of each vector is fixed and nonzero, so scalar-proportional unit vectors must have scalar $1$ and identical last-half signs; distinct code words therefore give distinct rays.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

derivations.claim: A gate of arity $r\le k$ has at most $W^r$ ordered wire tuples. Summing over possible arities $0\le r\le k$ gives at most $\sum_{r=0}^kW^r\le(k+1)W^k$ tuples because $W\ge1$; including its label gives at most $C_k A W^k$ choices for one occurrence.

A length-$g$ serial description is an ordered list of $g$ such choices, so there are at most $(C_k A W^k)^g$ descriptions. For two gates on disjoint supports, reorder the tensor factors as the first support, the second support, and the remaining wires. Their embeddings are then $G\otimes I\otimes I$ and $I\otimes H\otimes I$. By [F2], both compositions act as $Gx\otimes Hy\otimes z$ on elementary tensors, which span the register; thus they commute. By [F3], serially listing each layer therefore preserves its operator; listing the layers in circuit order preserves the full denotation and adds no occurrence.

citations.quote: Fix integers $W\ge1$, $A\ge1$, $k\ge1$, and $g\ge0$, and an ordered-wire circuit model with a finite gate alphabet of size $A$ and maximum arity $k$. A serial length-$g$ description is an ordered list of $g$ gate labels and ordered tuples of at most $k$ distinct wire positions; its denotation is the ordered product of the corresponding local gate embeddings. Each parallel layer consists of pairwise wire-disjoint occurrences and denotes their product. With $C_k=k+1$, the number of length-$g$ serial descriptions is at most $(C_k A W^k)^g$. Any parallel circuit with $g$ total occurrences has a serial ordering with the same gate count and denotation.

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
Then $\mathbb{R}$ is **uncountable** ([[def-countable]]): there is no surjection
$\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$, so $\mathbb{R}$ is neither finite nor countably
infinite.

The proof is Cantor's original argument of 1874, not the decimal diagonal.
Assuming a surjection $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$, one builds nested closed
intervals $[a_n, b_n]$ with $a_n < b_n$ and $f(n) \notin [a_{n+1}, b_{n+1}]$, and
then $\sup\{a_n\}$ is a real number that $f$ misses. **The decimal diagonal is
deliberately avoided**: decimal expansions are infinite series, which this
library has not yet constructed, so a diagonal proof here would rest on machinery
that does not exist. The diagonal argument survives in its non-circular form, on
power sets, as Cantor's theorem earlier on this page; see the remarks below.

**The construction uses no choice, and that is what the thirds are for.** Given
$[a_n, b_n]$ of length $d$, its three closed thirds
$[a_n, a_n + d/3]$, $[a_n + d/3, a_n + 2d/3]$, $[a_n + 2d/3, b_n]$ cannot all
contain $f(n)$, because the first and the third are disjoint; the rule takes the
**first one in that fixed order** which does not contain $f(n)$. That is a
definition by cases, so the whole construction is a single application of the
recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) to one explicitly given function. A version
of the argument that says "pick a third avoiding $f(n)$" would be using dependent
choice, silently and unnecessarily.

If $u$ is a unit representative, its associated operator is $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$, with the bra, ket and outer-product convention of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]]. derivations.claim: If $A=0$, the empty alphabet allows only the empty circuit, so at most one ray is reachable. If $A\ge1$, put $B=(k+1)AW^k\ge2$. Fix a finite listing of the alphabet and order wire tuples lexicographically; then [F1] gives at most $B^g$ descriptions of length $g\in\mathbb N$. Code each description by its length and its base-$B$ index, then pair these two natural numbers; this gives an injection of all finite descriptions into $\mathbb N$. In either case the reachable rays form a countable set without a choice principle.

These nonzero vectors define rays by [F3]. By [F2], the ray space is uncountable and cannot equal the countable reachable set.

Fix integers $W\ge1$, $A\ge1$, $k\ge1$, and $g\ge0$, and an ordered-wire circuit model with a finite gate alphabet of size $A$ and maximum arity $k$. A serial length-$g$ description is an ordered list of $g$ gate labels and ordered tuples of at most $k$ distinct wire positions; its denotation is the ordered product of the corresponding local gate embeddings. Each parallel layer consists of pairwise wire-disjoint occurrences and denotes their product. With $C_k=k+1$, the number of length-$g$ serial descriptions is at most $(C_k A W^k)^g$. Any parallel circuit with $g$ total occurrences has a serial ordering with the same gate count and denotation.

For unit vectors $u,v\in\mathbb C^D$,

$$d_{\mathrm{ch}}([u],[v])=\sqrt{2-2|\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}|}.$$

In particular, this value is independent of the chosen unit representatives, and it is zero exactly when the two vectors represent the same ray.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

derivations.claim: A single output ray cannot be within $\varepsilon$ of two distinct packed rays. Indeed, if $d_{\mathrm{ch}}([u],[q])\le\varepsilon$ and $d_{\mathrm{ch}}([v],[q])\le\varepsilon$, [F3] gives unit phases $\lambda,\mu$ with $\|u-\lambda q\|_2\le\varepsilon$ and $\|v-\mu q\|_2\le\varepsilon$; then [F4] gives $\|u-(\lambda/\mu)v\|_2\le2\varepsilon<2\sqrt\delta$, contradicting [F1]. Let $m\ge0$, $n\ge1$, and $r\ge1$ be integers, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$
be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a $C^r$ map with

$$ r>\max\{m-n,0\}. $$

Then the critical value set of $f$ is a null subset of $\mathbb R^n$.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $(K_i)_{i\ge0}$ be a sequence of compact null subsets of $\mathbb R^m$, where nullity is in the closed-cube-cover sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]. Then $\bigcup_{i\ge0}K_i$ is null. The proof selects finite rational-cube covers by their least codes and uses no choice principle.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.
For every integer $m\ge1$, every nonempty open subset $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is not null in the closed-cube-cover sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]. The proof uses no choice principle.

Let $n,a\ge0$ be integers and $D=2^n$. Let the data and workspace registers have ordered computational spaces $\mathbb C^D$ and $\mathbb C^{2^a}$, with the ordered tensor factors and product basis of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]. For a circuit unitary $U$ on their tensor product, its all-zero-workspace projection on a fixed input $|0^n\rangle|0^a\rangle$ is

$$v=(I_D\otimes\langle0^a|)U(|0^n\rangle\otimes|0^a\rangle)\in\mathbb C^D.$$

The projected joint vector is $v\otimes|0^a\rangle$. An exact clean-workspace output on this input means that the full, unconditional output equals $\lambda|\psi\rangle\otimes|0^a\rangle$ for a unit data vector $\psi$ and a unit scalar $\lambda$; then $v=\lambda\psi$. A merely nonzero $v$ defines only the zero-workspace projection branch and does not assert that the workspace is deterministically clean.

Fix $m\ge1$. A **closed cube** is a rectangle $\prod_{j<m}[a_j,a_j+\ell]$ with $\ell\ge0$; its volume is $\ell^m$. A set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **null** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is covered by a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at most $\varepsilon$. It has **content zero** when such a cover can be finite.

The series and finite sums are [[def-series]] and [[def-finite-sum]], and their nonnegative bounds use [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Both properties pass to subsets. Padding a finite cover with degenerate zero-volume cubes proves that content zero implies null. This terminology defines only cover-nullity; it does not define a measure on arbitrary sets.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to

**Input.** Integers $1\le D\le M$, ordered orthonormal bases of $\mathbb C^D$ and $\mathbb C^M$, and an exact $M\times D$ matrix $V$ whose columns are orthonormal, so $V$ represents a linear isometry in the convention of [[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]]. Arithmetic is ideal exact complex arithmetic with conjugation, norms, square roots, and exact zero tests; no bit-time bound is part of this procedure.

**Procedure.** Initialize an ordered list $L$ with the $D$ columns of $V$. For $j=0,1,\ldots,M-1$, compute

$$r_j=e_j-\sum_{w\in L}\langle e_j,w\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}w.$$

If $\|r_j\|_2=0$, leave $L$ unchanged. Otherwise append $r_j/\|r_j\|_2$ to $L$. After the finite loop, return the square matrix $W$ whose columns are the final list, and return INVALID if the input dimensions or orthonormal-column condition fail.

For integer widths $0\le n\le w$, put $D=2^n$, $M=2^w$, and $a=w-n$. The input data and clean workspace use the ordered tensor-register convention of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]] and the big-endian basis encoding of [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]]. A clean workspace register starts at $|0^a\rangle$ under [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]]. Let $\Pi$ be the ordered wire permutation that swaps the $n$-wire data block with the $a$-wire zero-workspace block, so $\Pi(|x\rangle|0^a\rangle)=|0^a\rangle|x\rangle$. This sends the declared clean-input basis to the first $D$ standard basis vectors. The matrix $W\Pi$ is the full-unitary extension interface used by [[thm-qc-isometry-completion-and-synthesis]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

For $n\ge0$ and a binary word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})\in\{0,1\}^n$, define its
**big-endian index**

$$\operatorname{enc}_n(x):=\sum_{k<n}x_k\,2^{\,n-1-k}.$$

Thus the first wire is the most significant bit. For $n=0$, the domain
$\{0,1\}^0$ consists only of the empty word $()$, and the empty sum gives
$\operatorname{enc}_0(())=0$. In an ordered $n$-qubit
computational basis, the word $x$ occupies the slot numbered
$\operatorname{enc}_n(x)$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

For $n\ge2$, every $n$-qubit unitary has an exact no-ancilla circuit with arbitrary one-qubit gates and at most
$$\frac{23}{48}4^n-\frac32 2^n+\frac43$$
CNOTs. For $n=0$ or $n=1$, no CNOT is needed. This is a gate-count bound; it makes no numerical decomposition-time or finite-precision bit-complexity claim.

derivations.claim: The initial list is orthonormal by the input hypothesis. If the current list is orthonormal, then for each $w_i\in L$ the residual satisfies $\langle r_j,w_i\rangle=\langle e_j,w_i\rangle-\sum_{w\in L}\langle e_j,w\rangle\langle w,w_i\rangle=0$ by [F2] and orthonormality. If it is nonzero, division by its positive norm gives a unit vector orthogonal to every previous column; if it is zero, $e_j$ already lies in their span. Thus each update preserves orthonormality and puts $e_j$ in the span of the updated list.

After the finite loop, every standard basis vector $e_j$ lies in the final span by step 1.1. The standard basis spans $\mathbb C^M$, so the final orthonormal list spans $\mathbb C^M$ and has exactly $M$ vectors. If $z=\sum_{j=1}^M c_jw_j$ is its expansion in that list, orthonormality and [F2] give $\|z\|_2^2=\sum_j|c_j|^2$; the same coordinate calculation for the standard basis gives $\|Wc\|_2^2=\sum_j|c_j|^2$. Thus the column map $W$ preserves norms and is injective by [F4]. By [F5] it is surjective in finite dimension, hence invertible; as a square norm-preserving map it is unitary by [F4]. Its first $D$ columns are the original list, namely $V$.

For $D=2^n$, $M=2^w$, [F3] identifies $|0^{w-n}\rangle|x\rangle$ with the standard basis vector $e_{\operatorname{enc}_n(x)}$ among the first $D$ vectors. The declared permutation obeys $\Pi(|x\rangle|0^{w-n}\rangle)=|0^{w-n}\rangle|x\rangle$. The first $D$ columns of $W$ then give $(W\Pi)(|x\rangle|0^{w-n}\rangle)=V|x\rangle$ for every computational basis input $x$; linearity gives the identity on the entire clean-input subspace.

The product $W\Pi$ is itself one $w$-qubit unitary, so applying the QSD interface [A1] directly to this matrix gives the stated full-unitary gate upper bound, with the $w=0,1$ cases treated separately. Because the permutation is absorbed into the target matrix before synthesis, no separate permutation gate count is added. The construction places no condition on the $M$ output coordinates beyond the isometry equation, so it makes no claim that the extra output wires are clean.

**Input and output.** Input an integer $n\ge0$ and an explicit exact table $(a_x)_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}$ in the ordered basis convention of [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]]. If the table length is not $D=2^n$ or $\sum_x|a_x|^2\ne1$, return INVALID. Otherwise return a finite continuous-gate circuit which prepares the ray $[a]$ from $|0^n\rangle$, together with its classical angle table. When the table is supplied as a dense fixed-width bit encoding, read all $b$ bits of each real and imaginary coordinate before computation. Arithmetic is ideal and exact: it supplies complex arithmetic, absolute value, exact zero tests and square roots; for $x,y\ge0$ not both zero, $\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)$ returns the unique $\phi\in[0,\pi/2]$ with $\cos\phi=x/\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and $\sin\phi=y/\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$. For $z\ne0$, $\arg z\in(-\pi,\pi]$ is the unique principal angle in the polar form of [[thm-polar-form-with-unique-principal-argument]], so $z=|z|e^{i\arg z}$ by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. No Turing bit-time bound is asserted.

**Prefix norms and rotations.** For every binary prefix $p$ of length at most $n$, set

$$r_p=\sqrt{\sum_{x\text{ extends }p}|a_x|^2}.$$

For $\theta\in\mathbb R$ define

$$R_y(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\theta/2)&-\sin(\theta/2)\\\sin(\theta/2)&\cos(\theta/2)\end{pmatrix}$$

in basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$. This is the $y$-axis rotation in the QC07 exponent convention; [[thm-qc-axis-rotation-pauli-formula]] gives this matrix and its unitarity. Define $C(U)=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,U)$ with the control as the first wire, following [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]]. For each $l=0,\ldots,n-1$ and each length-$l$ prefix $p$ in lexicographic order, skip the operation if $r_p=0$; otherwise set $\theta_p=2\operatorname{atan2}(r_{p1},r_{p0})$ and apply $R_y(\theta_p)$ to bit $l$, controlled on the first $l$ bits equaling $p$. Length zero means no control. Thus no division is performed on a zero-norm branch.

**Exact bounded-arity control construction.** For a control pattern with $m\ge2$ bits, conjugate each zero-control bit by $X$ so the desired condition becomes all ones. Allocate $m-1$ clean work bits $w_1,\ldots,w_{m-1}$. Compute $w_1=c_1c_2$ with one Toffoli; for $j=3,\ldots,m$, compute $w_{j-1}=w_{j-2}c_j$ with one Toffoli. Use the final work bit as the control for the desired two-wire unitary, then apply the Toffolis in reverse order and undo the $X$ conjugations. For a leaf phase, apply $P_\phi=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\phi})$ to the final work bit instead. For $m=1$ use the corresponding one-control unitary directly; for $m=0$ apply the one-qubit operation directly. The work bits return to zero after each operation and are reused. A one-bit leaf phase uses $P_\phi$ directly for pattern $1$ and $XP_\phi X$ for pattern $0$.

If an encoding assigns exactly $b$ bits to each real coordinate and $b$ bits to each imaginary coordinate, with basis order implicit, the dense table contains exactly $2Db$ input bits. Those bits must decode to the input table in an exact-table claim; finite-precision approximations are separate inputs with separate error hypotheses. The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Fix $k\ge1$, $U\in U(2^k)$, and a real $0<\varepsilon<1/2$. Suppose a supplied exact decomposition of
$U$ has $m\ge1$ one-qubit $U(2)$ factors and $c\ge0$ exact CNOT factors,
with no ancillas. Compiling the special-unitary part of each one-qubit factor
to error $\varepsilon/m$ gives a circuit $C$ such that
$$\min_{|\lambda|=1}\|U-\lambda C\|\le\varepsilon.$$
Its gate count is at most
$c+O(m\log^{\log_{3/2}5}(m/\varepsilon))$ for fixed $k$ and fixed base net.
For every unit vector $\psi$ and every nonnegative contraction $E$ on the
$2^k$-dimensional space, the event value
$p_E(V,\psi):=\|E^{1/2}V\psi\|^2$ changes by at most $2\varepsilon$ between
$V=U$ and $V=C$. The phase guarantee is for the whole unconditional block.
Here nonnegative contraction means $E=E^*$, $\langle Ev,v\rangle\ge0$ for
all $v$, and $\|E\|\le1$.

Use [F8] to choose a rational $\varepsilon'_c$ with $\varepsilon_c/2<\varepsilon'_c<\varepsilon_c$. Let the exact normalized-table circuit be $U_G\cdots U_1$. By [A1], for each whole block choose a unit scalar $\lambda_j$ and a compiled block $\widetilde U_j$ with $\|U_j-\lambda_j\widetilde U_j\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon'_c/G<\varepsilon_c/G$. Each block includes all of its controls and targets before compilation; thus $\lambda_j$ is a scalar on its entire support and becomes one global scalar when tensored with identities on the other wires.
Split the normalization error through $v$: by [F5], $\|v/\|v\|_2-a\|_2\le\|v/\|v\|_2-v\|_2+\|v-a\|_2=|1-\|v\|_2|+\|v-a\|_2\le2\eta$.

Insert the $G$ intermediate products between $U_G\cdots U_1$ and $(\prod_j\lambda_j)\widetilde U_G\cdots\widetilde U_1$ to obtain the telescoping sum with one block difference in each term. For any unit input vector, [F5] bounds the norm of the sum by the sum of term norms; [F6] gives norm $1$ for every surrounding unitary factor, so [F7] bounds each term by $\varepsilon'_c/G$. Applying this to the fixed initial vector gives projective chord error at most $\varepsilon'_c$ from the exact normalized-$v$ output.

By [F3], choose a phase aligning the compiled output to the exact normalized-$v$ joint output within $\varepsilon'_c$, and a phase aligning that exact output to $a\otimes|0^s\rangle$ within $2\eta$ by step 2.1. Multiplying the second phase by the first and applying [F5] gives $d_{\mathrm{ch}}([\mathrm{out}],[a\otimes|0^s\rangle])\le2\eta+\varepsilon'_c<2\eta+\varepsilon_c$.

Fix $m\ge1$. A **closed cube** is a rectangle $\prod_{j<m}[a_j,a_j+\ell]$ with $\ell\ge0$; its volume is $\ell^m$. A set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **null** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is covered by a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at most $\varepsilon$. It has **content zero** when such a cover can be finite.

The series and finite sums are [[def-series]] and [[def-finite-sum]], and their nonnegative bounds use [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Both properties pass to subsets. Padding a finite cover with degenerate zero-volume cubes proves that content zero implies null. This terminology defines only cover-nullity; it does not define a measure on arbitrary sets.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the
plane of pairs of naturals is countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

The bijection is exhibited, not merely asserted to exist. Define $2^m$ by
recursion on $m$ ([[thm-recursion]]) by $2^0 = 1$ and $2^{\sigma(m)} = 2^m + 2^m$,
and set

$$J(m,n) = 2^m \cdot \sigma(n + n), \qquad \text{that is} \qquad J(m,n) = 2^m(2n+1).$$

Then $J$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ onto
$\mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$, and $\sigma$ is a bijection from $\mathbb{N}$ onto
$\mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$, so $\sigma^{-1} \circ J$ is a bijection
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. What makes $J$ bijective is the
decomposition of a nonzero natural into a power of two times an odd number,
existence and uniqueness both.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals with $a_k \ge 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ be its partial sums and let
$S = \{\, s_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ be the range of $(s_n)$ ([[def-series]]).
Then:

1. $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing ([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and $s_n \ge 0$ for every
   $n$;
2. $\sum a_k$ converges **if and only if** $S$ is bounded above
   ([[def-bounded-set]]), and in that case
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;=\; \sup S ,$$
   so in particular $s_n \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k$ for every $n$;
3. if $S$ is not bounded above then $s_n \to +\infty$
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]) and $\sum a_k$ diverges.

This is the theorem that makes the nonnegative theory work: for terms of one
sign, convergence is a boundedness question and no candidate limit is ever
needed. Every comparison test on this page is an application of it.

Let $(N,0,\sigma)$ be a Peano system ([[def-peano-system]]), in particular the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). For any set $A$, any element $a \in A$, and any function $f : A \to A$, there is a unique function $g : N \to A$ such that $g(0) = a$ and $g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n))$ for all $n \in N$.

**Addition** $+ : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is defined by
recursion on the second argument: for each fixed $m \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$m + 0 = m, \qquad m + \sigma(n) = \sigma(m + n).$$

For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, define the **order** by

$$m \le n \iff \exists k \in \mathbb{N}\ (m + k = n),$$

and the **strict order** by $m < n \iff (m \le n \text{ and } m \neq n)$, using
addition ([[def-nat-addition]]).
The relation $\le$ on $\mathbb{N}$, where $m \le n \iff \exists k\ (m + k = n)$ ([[def-nat-order]]), is a linear (total) order: reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive, and total.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, let $d$ be the
unique natural number satisfying $m+d=n+1$. Existence is the definition of
natural order ([[def-nat-order]]); if $m+d=m+e$, commutativity
([[lem-nat-add-commutative]]) gives $d+m=e+m$, so cancellation
([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]) gives $d=e$. On these admissible bounds only,
we may write this unique additive gap as $d=n+1-m$; no total natural subtraction
operation is presupposed. With $d$ thus fixed, define

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Equivalently, for naturals $m \le r$, the half-open endpoint notation
$\sum_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ and $\prod_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ means
$\sum_{j<d}a_{m+j}$ and $\prod_{j<d}a_{m+j}$, respectively, where $d$ is the
unique natural with $m+d=r$. Here $r-1$ is an endpoint label for the terms
before $r$, so this notation needs no total subtraction operation. For $m=r$,
the unique gap is $0$ because $m+0=m$, giving the empty sum and product; the
case $m=r=0$ is the $-1$ endpoint convention just stipulated.

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

derivations.claim: Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be compact and null, and let $\eta>0$. If $K=\varnothing$, the empty family covers it. Otherwise [F1] gives a countable closed-cube cover $(C_j)$ with total volume at most $\eta/8$. Write $C_j=\prod_{r<m}[a_{jr},a_{jr}+\ell_j]$ and let $x_{jr}=a_{jr}+\ell_j/2$ be its center coordinates. Set $\delta_j=\min\{1,\eta2^{-j-5}/(3^m(1+\ell_j)^{m-1})\}$ and let $C'_j=\prod_{r<m}(x_{jr}-(\ell_j+2\delta_j)/2,x_{jr}+(\ell_j+2\delta_j)/2)$, an open concentric enlargement. By the binomial formula, $(\ell_j+2\delta_j)^m-\ell_j^m=\sum_{r=1}^{m}\binom mr\ell_j^{m-r}(2\delta_j)^r\le\delta_j(1+\ell_j)^{m-1}\sum_{r=1}^{m}\binom mr2^r<3^m\delta_j(1+\ell_j)^{m-1}\le\eta2^{-j-5}$, because $\delta_j^r\le\delta_j$, $\ell_j^{m-r}\le(1+\ell_j)^{m-1}$ and $\sum_{r=1}^m\binom mr2^r=3^m-1$. Define the covering cost of an open cube of side $s$ to be $s^m$; this agrees with [F5] for its closed counterpart. The open cubes cover $K$ and their total covering cost is at most $\eta/8+\eta/16=3\eta/16<\eta/4$, using the geometric series. Compactness [F2] gives a finite subcover.

Order the finite subcover by its original indices and write $L_r$ and $x_r$ for the side and center of its $r$th open cube. The finite polynomial sum $\sum_r(L_r+\zeta)^m$ is continuous at $\zeta=0$, so choose $\zeta>0$ for which it is less than $\sum_rL_r^m+\eta/8<3\eta/8$. By [F4], choose rational $q_r$ with $L_r<q_r<L_r+\zeta$ and a rational center $y_r\in\mathbb Q^m$ whose coordinates differ from $x_r$ by less than $(q_r-L_r)/4$. The closed rational cube of side $q_r$ centered at $y_r$ contains the open cube of side $L_r$ centered at $x_r$, since each coordinate displacement is less than $L_r/2+(q_r-L_r)/4<q_r/2$. These finitely many rational cubes cover $K$, and their total volume is less than $3\eta/8<\eta/2$ by [F5].

Fix a bijection $\nu:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Q$ and a pairing bijection $\pi:\mathbb N^2\to\mathbb N$ from [F3]. A list of $t$ rational cubes is determined by $(m+1)t$ rationals: its side and its $m$ center coordinates for each cube. Encode a tuple $(a_0,\ldots,a_{r-1})\in\mathbb N^r$ recursively by $c_0=0$ and $c_{r+1}(a_0,\ldots,a_r)=\pi(a_0,c_r(a_1,\ldots,a_r))$. Since $\pi$ and $\nu$ are injective, pairing the list length $t$ with the code of its $(m+1)t$ rational coordinates gives an injection from all finite rational cube lists into $\mathbb N$. For each natural code, use its unique list preimage if it has one, and otherwise use the empty list; this defines an enumeration $(\mathcal C_s)_{s\ge0}$ that includes every list. By step 2.1, every compact null $K$ has at least one enumerated list covering it with total volume less than $\eta/2$. The set of qualifying codes is nonempty, so it has a least member by [F6]. The least-code rule assigns a unique cover to each pair $(K,\eta)$ without choosing from an arbitrary family.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. For each $i\ge0$, apply the unique rule of step 3.1 to $(K_i,\eta_i)$ with $\eta_i=\varepsilon2^{-i-1}$. Let $t_i$ be the finite length of its selected list, whose total volume is less than $\varepsilon2^{-i-2}$. Define $N_0=0$ and $N_{i+1}=N_i+t_i$ recursively as in [F8]. For each $n\in\mathbb N$, if $N_i\le n<N_{i+1}$ for some $i$, take the cube at position $n-N_i$ in the $i$th list; otherwise take the degenerate zero-side cube at the origin. The half-open index intervals are disjoint: if $i<j$, then $N_{i+1}\le N_j$, so no $n$ lies in both. Each cube of the $i$th list, at position $j<t_i$, occurs at index $N_i+j$; thus every selected list occurs in the sequence.

Any finite initial segment meets only finitely many blocks. If it meets none, its total volume is zero. Otherwise, its finite set of block indices has a largest member $r$: scan the finite list and retain the larger at each comparison using the linear order in [F8]. Each partial block costs at most its full-list bound from step 4.1. By [F9], the budget sum $B_r=\sum_{i=0}^{r}\varepsilon2^{-i-2}$ satisfies $B_0=\varepsilon/4=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}(1-2^{-1})$ and $B_{r+1}=B_r+\varepsilon2^{-r-3}=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}(1-2^{-r-1})+\varepsilon2^{-r-3}=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}(1-2^{-r-2})$. So induction gives $B_r=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}(1-2^{-r-1})<\varepsilon/2$. Thus every partial sum of the nonnegative volume series is at most $\varepsilon/2$, and [F7] gives convergence with total at most $\varepsilon/2<\varepsilon$. The sequence covers $\bigcup_iK_i$, so [F1] shows that this union is null. Since every selected list is assigned by the unique least-code rule of step 3.1, the proof uses no choice principle.
